competency_fulfillment.rationale: The illustrate half is really there: seed 42 sets up 'A rectangle is covered edge-to-edge with unit square tiles, arranged in 2 rows and 7 columns' and seed 55 puts a picture in front of the student with 'Look at the 4×3 array. How many squares are shaded in all?', so area is always reached by counting square tile units. The estimate half is only a word. Seed 50 says 'Estimate how many unit tiles cover the square in all.' but offers 8, 16, 15 and 17, and seed 45 asks 'About how many tiles in total will you use?' against 26, 10, 25 and 20 — no estimation strategy separates 25 from 26, so the hedged wording demands an exact product while teaching the student that estimating means computing exactly.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both figures the competency names are tiled and both are asked about: the square at seed 44, 'A square is covered edge-to-edge with unit square tiles, arranged in 2 rows and 2 columns', and the rectangle at seed 606, 'A rectangle is covered edge-to-edge with unit square tiles, arranged in 4 rows and 7 columns'. The illustrated presentation that the verb illustrate calls for is carried by the array items, seed 605 'Look at the 5×6 array.' and seed 500 'Look at the 10×10 array.', and seed 601 takes the same tiling idea onto a real surface, 'Pia wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 2 m long and 3 m wide with square tiles that are 1 m on each side'.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Each stem holds one array in one clause, so the reasoning is a single count or product: seed 502, 'You are laying unit square tiles over a square, fitting 3 rows and 3 columns exactly', needs only 3 × 3. The one word problem, seed 601, 'Pia wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 2 m long and 3 m wide with square tiles that are 1 m on each side', is fully answerable from the information given — both side lengths and the tile size are stated, giving 2 × 3 = 6 — with no hidden conversion and no leftover partial tile for a Grade 3 Quarter 1 pupil to reason about.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Four genuinely different presentations appear across the fourteen samples, not one template renumbered: the third-person tiling report at seed 43, 'A rectangle is covered edge-to-edge with unit square tiles, arranged in 7 rows and 4 columns'; the second-person action framing at seed 602, 'You are laying unit square tiles over a rectangle, fitting 5 rows and 3 columns exactly'; the read-the-picture items such as seed 55, 'Look at the 4×3 array', which name no rows or columns in prose and force the student to read the arrangement off the figure; and the contextual garden item at seed 601. Three formatters (mcq, cloze, read_mcq) carry them.

competency_alignment.rationale: Every sample keeps the square tile as the unit of measure and asks only how many of them cover the figure — seed 46, 'A rectangle is covered edge-to-edge with unit square tiles, arranged in 2 rows and 5 columns', and seed 605, 'Look at the 5×6 array. How many squares are shaded in all?'. Nothing drifts to perimeter, nothing states an area and asks back for a missing side, and no stem hands the student a rule to apply; even the contextual item at seed 601 measures with 'square tiles that are 1 m on each side', so the tile remains the unit rather than a length formula.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: The arithmetic each sample actually demands stays inside the multiplication facts to ten: 2 × 2 = 4 at seed 44, 7 × 4 = 28 at seed 43, 4 × 7 = 28 at seed 606, and the largest is the array at seed 500, 'Look at the 10×10 array', a hundred-square whose answer 100 is the familiar Grade 3 hundred chart. No sample needs a two-digit by two-digit product, and the garden at seed 601 is 2 m long and 3 m wide, a size a Grade 3 pupil can picture.
